title: Thalassa Global - OnPrem Egress, Data Residency & KMS Review
summary: Deep technical discussion focused on on-prem/VPC deployment constraints: egress control requirements for European data residency, KMS/HSM integration for per-customer keys, audit log retention for SOC 2 evidence, and RBAC/SSO mapping for Redwood Console. Agreed next steps include a short pilot design doc, an egress firewall diagram from Thalassa, and a joint KMS PoC plan.

transcript:
Meeting Header:
Date: 2026-02-17
Start: 15:00 PST
Duration: 62 minutes
Attendees: Samira Chen (Redwood AE), Diego Morales (Redwood SE), Priya Rao (Redwood Solutions Eng); Liam O'Connell (CISO), Marta Ruiz (Cloud Architect), Anand Patel (Compliance Lead), Yvonne Kim (Network Engineer)

Auto-generated Summary (may be imperfect): high level discussion about on prem deployment, egress controls, kms and key management, audit logging retention for soc2 and iso, rbac and sso mapping for the redwood console and private control plane.

Transcript: 
[00:00] Samira: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick audio check?
[00:04] Liam: Yep, we're good. Sorry this is a bit of a cross timezone call for some of us.
[00:08] Marta: all good, can hear you Samira.
[00:12] Samira: Great. Goal today: walk through Thalassa's egress and data residency needs, KMS options, and how audit logs map to SOC 2 controls. We'll have Diego go into some network diagrams. Diego take it away.
[00:25] Diego: Sure. So uh, quick caveat I might mispronounce a couple things - our private offering is Redwood Private (sometimes the transcription shows Redwood Privatey, sorry). On-prem or VPC deployment basically gives you a private control plane and we run the inference runtime in your environment or in a dedicated pool.
[00:40] Diego: For egress, there are two main patterns we see: 1) tightly locked egress with allowlists for specific model artifact registries and telemetry endpoints, and 2) zero-Internet egress where customers want all model downloads pre-staged and no external DNS resolution.
[00:58] Yvonne: For Thalassa regulatory reasons in EU, we need all inference logs and prompt/response material to remain in region and never transit US. We are also required to firewall any telemetry that goes out.
[01:12] Diego: Understood. We can route model traffic to regional model variants and pin runtime to regional images. For telemetry, Redwood can be configured to send only anonymized aggregate metrics out, or you can disable outbound telemetry entirely.
[01:28] Marta: On the KMS side, we need a customer-managed key (CMK) in our Azure Key Vault / HSM. We want encryption-at-rest for model weights plus per-customer envelope keys so that in an audit, we can demonstrate separation of keys.
[01:44] Diego: We support two patterns: a) Redwood-managed key wrap where Redwood holds the envelope keys but integrates with your KMS for root unwrap, and b) fully customer-managed KMS where your vault issues keys and the runtime has a minimal wrapper that calls your KMS for unwrap operations. The latter meets stricter compliance but requires network access from runtime to KMS (or a private link).
[02:05] Anand: If we do fully customer-managed KMS, what about key rotation and access logs? Our auditor wants evidence of rotation policies and logged decryption events tied to identities.
[02:19] Priya: We can emit key usage events into your SIEM by forwarding audit logs. For the customer-managed route, the KMS logs live in your environment. For Redwood-managed wrap, we provide key rotation windows and we publish rotation events to our audit log which you can pull via the Private control plane API.
[02:36] Liam: We need to be crystal on who has ability to decrypt. In our threat model, minimal people inside Redwood should be able to access plaintext. Can we implement split knowledge or HSM-backed approvals?
[02:48] Diego: For HSM-backed approvals you can tie the unwrap operation to HSM policies; however, the runtime still needs the ability to call unwrap. We can lock that behind a service identity that you control via IAM and RBAC. We also support optional 'seal/unseal' flows that require an out-of-band approval for key import.
[03:06] Marta: On network side, we use egress gateways that do deep packet inspection and terminate TLS for outgoing traffic to external registries. We need to see the exact IP ranges and FQDNs Redwood will talk to.
[03:20] Samira: We'll share a consolidated list of IP ranges, FQDNs and Azure Private Link endpoints. Diego, can you capture the list and add recommended firewall rules?
[03:28] Diego: Yup, I'll draft the recommended security group rules. We'll include explicit ports, ranges, and FQDNs. Note that if you pre-stage model blobs into your internal registry, you'll reduce egress to zero for model downloads.
[03:40] Yvonne: Pre-staging is preferred. Two questions: can the runtime fetch model updates from internal artifact repo without access to external registries? And, can we disable DNS egress entirely and use IP allow?
[03:54] Priya: Yes to both. We support pulling from internal artifact registries and you can set exact IPs. The only caveat is for model telemetry and heartbeats; if those are disabled or routed to your collector, we lose some observability on performance.
[04:10] Liam: For SOC 2, we need evidence that logs are immutable and retained for 12 months. What forms of audit logging does Redwood provide in Private?
[04:22] Diego: Private control plane emits operation logs, API access logs, model serve events, and a per-request trace that includes request id, model variant, and timestamps. Those logs can be shipped to your logging infra (we support S3/GCS/ADLS exporters and syslog/forwarders). We also have an append-only storage option for compliance customers.
[04:40] Marta: Is the per-request transcript (prompts/responses) logged by default? We need to control PII.
[04:48] Priya: By default, request transcripts are stored for X days for debugging, but you can disable request body retention and only store metadata. We also provide redaction hooks to scrub PII from logs before storage.
[05:02] Anand: Our auditors will ask for sample evidence — can you provide a sample log export and mapping to SOC 2 control IDs?
[05:10] Samira: Yes, I'll attach the SOC 2 mapping doc. Diego, can you include a sanitized sample export?
[05:16] Diego: Will do. I'll attach one with fake request ids and masked content.
[05:20] Marta: About SSO and RBAC, we use Okta and have groups mapped to environment roles. We need console access limited to a handful of people; everything else should go through API service accounts.
[05:32] Priya: We support SAML/SSO with Okta, SCIM provisioning for groups, and role mappings. You can map Okta groups to Redwood roles and restrict console access. For Private, you can also disable the console UI entirely and only allow API tokens via your KMS-backed signing.
[05:48] Yvonne: Does that mean we can rotate service account tokens automatically? We want tokens with short TTLs and automatic rotation through our Vault.
[05:55] Diego: Yes, we can integrate with Vault for dynamic secrets, or you can push short-lived credentials via a bootstrap process.
[06:03] Liam: On network segmentation, we run a zero-trust model. The runtime should only talk to KMS and internal artifact repo. Any telemetry to Redwood must be explicitly allowed. Can we get a runbook for incident response if a node attempts to reach an unknown external host?
[06:17] Priya: We'll provide an incident playbook. Typical steps: isolate node, capture PCAP, collect runtime logs, rotate keys if KMS compromise suspected, and k-scan to ensure no rogue containers. We can also integrate with your SOAR for automated isolation.
[06:34] Marta: One subtlety: our compliance team requires proof that model weights are stored only in the EU region; can you guarantee regional pinning for model storage and runtime placement?
[06:45] Diego: Yes; for Private deployments we can ensure the runtime and model store live on nodes in your EU region. For hosted variants we have regional deployments but need contractual data residency clauses.
[06:58] Yvonne: For egress firewalling we use both allowlist of FQDNs and TLS interception - will Redwood support certificate pinning or do you break TLS?
[07:09] Diego: We don't break TLS on customer side by default. If your egress appliance terminates TLS, that's on your side. Redwood's outbound calls use TLS to the registries. If you need to intercept, you'll have to supply certs or operate a proxy we trust (mutual TLS).
[07:24] Anand: Regarding mutual TLS, can Redwood authenticate to our proxy using client certs that we rotate?
[07:30] Diego: Yes, we support mTLS and client cert rotation. The runtime reads certs from a mounted secret or from your vault depending on how you want to provision them.
[07:38] Samira: Quick pause — I want to cover fallback behaviour. If KMS is temporarily unavailable, what's the degrade path?
[07:44] Diego: The runtime won't be able to unwrap new keys; in that case we fail closed for decryption operations to avoid leaking. For cached keys in memory we can serve existing sessions until TTL expires. We can also configure a read-only cached unwrap that requires a short-lived cached envelope key, but that reduces security.
[08:02] Marta: Our auditors prefer fail-closed.
[08:05] Diego: Noted. We'll default to fail-closed for Thalassa.
[08:09] Yvonne: About retention periods: we need 12 months immutable for audit logs, but only 30 days for request bodies. Is that configurable per-customer?
[08:19] Priya: Yes, we can configure retention windows per tenant and also specify which artifacts are immutable. For append-only storage we can send a digest to your WORM storage.
[08:30] Liam: Any dependencies on cloud provider features for archive? We use Azure with GRS replication, does Redwood integrate with that?
[08:36] Diego: We can export to ADLS Gen2 or storage accounts. If you want GRS, it'll be your storage account settings; Redwood writes into the container/path you provide.
[08:48] Marta: A couple of operational questions: 1) how do we prove to a regulator that Palo Alto firewall rules weren't changed mid-audit? 2) can we get an immutable snapshot of firewall rules?
[08:58] Samira: Typically customers capture config snapshots into version control and we tie change events to a certifying user. We can help automate snapshots and time-stamp them in your archival store.
[09:10] Anand: We also want to know who inside Redwood would have support access to the Private control plane during onboarding.
[09:17] Samira: For onboarding, we have a named support engineer list and we can operate under an MSA/Support agreement. Access is scoped, logged, and can be time-limited. We can also do jumpbox sessions monitored by your team.
[09:29] Diego: Adding to that - all admin actions are logged with user id and IP. We can provide a filtered stream of those admin actions.
[09:36] Yvonne: About the model artifacts: if we pre-stage blobs, how do we do version pinning and rollback?
[09:43] Diego: We support versioned manifests and an immutable blob store approach. Rollbacks are a manifest switch operation that we can automate and log.
[09:52] Marta: I want to dig into the KMS PoC plan - can we map the flow? Example: model decryption at runtime -> unwrap with customer KMS -> decrypt envelope -> load into process. What's the exact footprint?
[10:04] Diego: Flow is exactly that. The runtime process requests unwrap from your KMS via a service identity; KMS returns a plaintext envelope key (optionally HSM-protected), runtime decrypts model blob locally, then zeroes keys from memory when done. We instrument the runtime to do secure memory wipe.
[10:20] Priya: Note: we also support mmap/no-mmap options to limit memory persistence depending on your platform.
[10:25] Yvonne: Will that require kernel modules or extra privileges?
[10:28] Diego: On Linux, secure memory options may require CAP_SYS_ADMIN for certain mmap flags; we document required capabilities. For the safest mode you can run with a small, dedicated runtime instance that we help you harden.
[10:40] Liam: Let's talk about network policy enforcement inside the cluster. We use Calico with eBPF. Can Redwood runtime labels integrate with our network policies?
[10:50] Diego: Yes, we annotate pods/nodes with labels and support a CNI-friendly approach. We provide a daemonset that applies the correct labels so your Calico policies can match.
[10:59] Marta: For isolation, we want each tenant to run in its own namespace and veth sandbox. Do you support multi-tenant isolation in the same VPC?
[11:08] Diego: Yes, using Kubernetes namespaces with network policy isolation or separate node pools. We also support dedicated GPU node pools per tenant for stronger isolation.
[11:18] Anand: Any recommended hardening guide for the runtime OS?
[11:22] Priya: We have a runtime hardening checklist: minimal packages, SCAP benchmarks, Host IPS, kernel livepatch strategy. We'll share that.
[11:30] Yvonne: Back to egress: can Redwood operate through a private link to your artifact store, like Azure Private Link endpoints?
[11:36] Diego: Yes, Private Link is supported. We can configure runtime to use Private Link endpoints to your registry and KMS private endpoints.
[11:44] Marta: For the PoC, what access do you need from our side?
[11:48] Samira: Minimal: a dev VPC with a test artifact repo, a test KMS key with limited permissions, and a service account for the runtime. We'll do a short-lived window and revoke after PoC.
[11:59] Liam: About telemetry, if we disable outbound telemetry to Redwood, how do we perform operational troubleshooting with Redwood support?
[12:07] Diego: You can enable selective telemetry or provide a read-only view into your metrics. Alternatively we can operate with a sidecar that forwards sanitized metrics to Redwood.
[12:16] Marta: Are there contractual clauses for data handling? For instance, if an incident occurs, what's your notification SLA?
[12:23] Samira: Incident notification SLAs are part of enterprise contracts. Typical is 1 hour for severity 1, with post-incident reports. We'll surface our standard terms and can negotiate tighter windows.
[12:33] Yvonne: One more item - we want to ensure the Private control plane does not egress telemetry that includes client prompt content. Is there an option to never transmit prompt content off-prem?
[12:42] Priya: Yes, prompt content can be disabled from leaving the environment. You can choose to only send anonymized performance telemetry.
[12:49] Anand: For audit evidence, we asked for a sample runbook earlier. Can Redwood provide a table mapping log types to SOC 2 criteria and sample export lines?
[12:58] Diego: We'll include that in the deliverables. We'll redact PII but show the fields and control mapping.
[13:04] Samira: OK, let's recap next steps briefly. Diego will prepare the KMS integration options doc and a sample sanitized log. Marta will share firewall rules and VPC diagrams. Samira will circulate SOC 2 mapping doc and the Private deployment compliance pack.
[13:19] Liam: Sounds good. One last question - any blockers we should be aware of to start a 2-week pilot?
[13:25] Diego: No major blockers. Access to a test KMS, a test artifact repo and a list of IP allow requirements is everything we need.
[13:32] Marta: We'll get those to you by end of next week.
[13:36] Samira: Great. Thanks everybody, we'll follow up with an email and attach the docs.
[13:40] Yvonne: Thanks all.
[13:42] Meeting ended.
